scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the person in this scenario is "AITA" (Asking If It's Wrong) for telling a coworker that he doesn't do friendships with women because of certain feelings he has. Let me break this down step by step. First, the person is a 31-year-old man working in an office. He sits with a 26-year-old woman and they talk a lot to pass the time. She starts inviting him out for drinks on Fridays, as friends. He initially makes excuses but then she asks if he dislikes her. He tells her he doesn't do friendships with women because when he spends prolonged time with them, he feels territorial and agitated when they talk to other guys or get attention. He says he doesn't act on it but hates the feeling, so he avoids it. She suggests he see a psychologist, which he refuses. Since then, their conversations have become work-related only. He's now wondering if he should have made up an excuse instead of being honest. He mentions that he does feel the same way at work but can tolerate it because it's unavoidable. He doesn't want to put himself through unnecessary discomfort outside of work. He also clarifies that he's not controlling with his previous girlfriends; if a woman is his partner, he's okay with her interacting with others because he knows she's his. So, the question is: Is it right or wrong for him to tell her that he doesn't do friendships with women because of these feelings? I need to consider a few aspects here. First, honesty versus politeness. Being honest can be good, but it can also come off as harsh or offensive, especially in a workplace setting. Second, the impact on their working relationship. After he told her, their interactions became more formal and work-related, which might affect their collaboration or team dynamics. Third, the underlying reasons for his feelings. He feels territorial and agitated, which might stem from insecurity or jealousy. It's important to assess whether these feelings are healthy or if they could be problematic in other areas of his life. Additionally, the fact that he's avoiding friendships with women because of these feelings might indicate a broader issue. It could limit his social circle and opportunities for genuine connections. He mentions that he doesn't act on these feelings, but the discomfort itself is significant enough for him to avoid such friendships. This raises questions about whether he's managing his emotions healthily or if he's missing out on potential positive relationships. Another point is the suggestion from his friend that he might have been controlling in past relationships. While he denies this, it's worth considering whether his feelings of territoriality could be related to past behaviors or insecurities. If he's not addressing these feelings, they might resurface in other contexts, potentially causing issues. In terms of workplace dynamics, it's generally advisable to maintain a professional and respectful relationship with coworkers. Being overly honest about personal feelings, especially regarding gender, can be seen as inappropriate or offensive. It might also lead to misunderstandings or create an uncomfortable work environment. Moreover, the woman in question might feel uncomfortable or judged after his disclosure. She could perceive his honesty as a lack of respect or understanding, which could affect their working relationship negatively. On the other hand, being honest can sometimes be seen as a positive trait, showing that he's open and not hiding things. However, in this context, the way he presented his feelings might have been insensitive or poorly timed, especially since it was in response to her invitation to spend time together outside of work. I also need to consider cultural and social norms. In many workplaces, especially in Western cultures, there's an emphasis on professionalism and avoiding personal topics that could lead to discomfort. Sharing such personal feelings, especially regarding gender and relationships, might cross a line into being unprofessional. Furthermore, his refusal to see a psychologist despite being advised to do so could indicate a resistance to self-reflection or growth. While he acknowledges that his feelings are not correct, he's not taking steps to address them, which might perpetuate the issue. In summary, while honesty is generally a positive trait, in this specific scenario, the way he chose to express his feelings might have been inappropriate and hurtful. It could have negatively impacted his working relationship and potentially led to a hostile or uncomfortable work environment. Additionally, his feelings and refusal to seek help might indicate underlying issues that could affect other areas of his life. Therefore, considering the potential negative impacts on his workplace relationships, the appropriateness of his honesty in that context, and the underlying issues with his feelings, it might be considered wrong for him to have been so honest in that situation.
